title: MLOps / ML platform engineer
summary: A curated sequence over the library for a MLOps / ML platform engineer: 35 lessons in 9 modules, from the foundations of the role to its advanced topics.

modules.title: Foundations of the ML platform role
modules.intro: This module sets the base for the ML platform role: what MLOps adds to ordinary software delivery, and the Python, Kubernetes and AWS skills every later module builds on. Each lesson starts with the concept, then moves to how teams run it in production and which tools implement it.

modules.title: Data and feature infrastructure
modules.intro: This module covers the data layer under an ML platform: the batch and streaming compute that builds datasets, the stores that hold them, and the feature store that serves the same values to training and inference. Each lesson starts from the architecture and then goes into the operating details a platform engineer owns, such as partitioning, cost, correctness over time and failure recovery.

modules.title: Workflow orchestration
modules.intro: Workflow orchestration is the layer that turns individual ML steps such as ingestion, feature computation, training, evaluation and deployment into repeatable, observable, retryable pipelines. This module covers the general-purpose scheduler most teams start with (Airflow), the ML-native orchestrators built around containers and artifacts, and durable execution with Temporal for long-running, event-driven processes.

modules.title: Training infrastructure
modules.intro: Training infrastructure is the part of an ML platform that turns expensive GPU hardware into repeatable, traceable training runs. This module covers how runs are recorded, how GPUs are exposed to Kubernetes, how one job spans many nodes, and how a shared cluster decides who runs when.

modules.title: Model release engineering
modules.intro: Model release engineering covers the path from a trained artifact to a version serving production traffic: how the model is packaged and versioned, what evidence it must produce before promotion, and how automation moves it through environments. The lessons go from registry and evaluation gates through CI/CD and GitOps to progressive rollout and rollback.

modules.title: Serving and inference
modules.intro: This module covers how trained models become reliable inference services: the architecture of online and batch serving, the managed route through SageMaker, and the specialised runtimes used for large language models. It moves from general serving patterns to LLM engines and then to compilation, quantization and edge targets, where latency and cost are won.

modules.title: LLM and agent platform
modules.intro: This module covers the platform layer that sits between application teams and large language models: hosted model APIs, retrieval infrastructure, agent runtimes with tool protocols, and the operational discipline that keeps them measurable and safe. It moves from calling a model, to grounding it in data, to letting it act, to proving that all of it works in production.

modules.title: Operating ML in production
modules.intro: This module covers what happens after a model ships: seeing what it does, knowing when it degrades, keeping it reliable, keeping it secure, and paying a sensible price for it. Each lesson starts from the operating principle and then moves to the concrete tools and configuration a platform team uses.

modules.title: Designing the platform as a product
modules.intro: An ML platform succeeds only if teams choose to use it, so this module treats the platform as a product with users, paved paths and measurable adoption. It then covers the system design needed to share that platform safely across many tenants, and the written decision process that keeps its architecture coherent.

steps.module: Foundations of the ML platform role
steps.why: MLOps applies DevOps discipline to systems whose behavior depends on data and trained artifacts as well as code.

steps.module: Foundations of the ML platform role
steps.why: Python is the common language of ML teams, so platform tooling, pipeline components and SDKs are mostly written in it.

steps.module: Foundations of the ML platform role
steps.why: Kubernetes is the default substrate for ML platforms because it schedules containers across a shared pool of machines and keeps declared state true.

steps.module: Foundations of the ML platform role
steps.why: Amazon EKS is the managed Kubernetes service many ML platforms are built on: AWS runs the control plane and the team owns the workloads, the node strategy and the integrations.
Apache Spark is the default engine for building training sets and feature tables that do not fit on one machine.

ML systems use several stores, each chosen for one access pattern: object storage and lakehouse tables for bulk training data, a warehouse for analytical SQL, a relational database for metadata and transactional state, and a key-value store for low-latency lookups at inference.
A feature store is the system that defines features once and serves the same values to training and to online inference.
Airflow models a pipeline as a DAG of tasks defined in Python, and a scheduler decides when each task runs based on a schedule, dependencies and state.
ML-native orchestrators treat a pipeline as a graph of containerized, typed steps that produce versioned artifacts, rather than as scheduled tasks that happen to run ML code.
Temporal provides durable execution: workflow code runs as if failures do not exist, because every step is recorded in an event history and the workflow can be rebuilt by replay after a crash.
Experiment tracking records what was run, with which inputs, and what came out, so any model can be traced back to its code, data and hyperparameters.
Kubernetes does not understand GPUs natively; it learns about them through a device plugin that advertises them as an extended resource.
When a model or dataset is too large for one GPU, training is spread across several GPUs and several nodes that must start together, find each other and stay in sync.
A shared GPU cluster has more demand than capacity, so something must decide which jobs run, in what order, and on whose budget.

A model registry is the system of record between training and serving: it gives each trained artifact a name, an immutable version, lineage back to the run that produced it, and a state that says whether it may be deployed.
An evaluation gate turns the question of whether a model is good enough into an automated, repeatable check that blocks promotion when it fails.
CI/CD for machine learning extends ordinary software delivery with two extra artifacts, data and models, and a third loop, continuous training.
Reproducible environments come from declaring everything in version control and letting automation converge real systems toward it.

Offline evaluation cannot prove a model behaves well on live traffic, so releases are staged: the new version is exposed to production conditions gradually while automated checks decide whether to continue.
Model serving turns a versioned model artifact into an inference API with defined latency, throughput and availability.
Amazon SageMaker offers managed hosting in which AWS runs the instances, load balancing and health management while the team supplies a container and a model artifact.
Serving open-weight LLMs is a distinct discipline because generation is autoregressive: each request holds GPU memory for its whole lifetime and produces output token by token.
When latency or hardware budget is tight, the model itself is optimised for the target device instead of only scaling the service around it.
Hosted LLMs turn model serving into an API integration problem: the platform team does not run GPUs, but it owns access, quotas, cost, latency and the contract that application code uses.
Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a model's parametric knowledge with an external, searchable store, so answers can be grounded in current and private data and can cite it.
An agent is a model that decides its own next step in a loop of reasoning, tool calls and observations, as opposed to a workflow whose steps are fixed in code.
LLMOps applies the release and operations discipline of MLOps to systems whose behavior is set by prompts, models, retrieval and tools together.
Observability is the ability to explain a system's internal state from the telemetry it emits, without shipping new code to ask a new question.
A model can be up, fast and error-free while its predictions get worse, because the data it sees has moved away from the data it was trained on.

Reliability practice turns the vague goal of a stable service into numbers and routines: service level objectives that define good enough, alerts tied to those objectives, an on-call rotation with runbooks, and postmortems that turn incidents into fixes.
An ML platform concentrates valuable things: training data, model weights, expensive compute and credentials to many systems.
ML workloads are expensive and bursty, so capacity has to follow demand at two levels: the number of pods and the number and type of nodes under them.
